full_judgment: 7. Mr Hafizullah submits that the prescription above inures generally to the benefit of the plaintiff by enabling the plaintiff to add as parties to a suit anyone or entity or body who may and can possibly meet the plaintiff's claim, qualified, of course, by the demands of the facts and circumstances of any given case. He submits, however, that in the present instance and as is evident in the objections raised as to locus standi, the plaintiff is inclined to further read into that enabling provision an underlying absolute requirement of participation in a suit, where necessary, only through fully scrutinised and ascertained representation. In this regard, both Mr Hafizullah and the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 5 Dr M Zahir further lay stress on yet another provision of the Code, i.e. Order VII, rule 1 as, in stipulating the essential components of a plaint, states that, among other things, the plaint shall contain the name, description and place of residence of the defendants, "so far as they can be ascertained". Drawing this Court's attention to the manner in which the defendant Nos. 5 and 15 have, in particular, been described in the plaint itself identifying both these parties in their individual and representative character, thereby, raising the presumption that such description followed upon some enquiry and ascertainment by and satisfaction of the plaintiff itself of the existence of a principal-agent relationship or, at the very least, of the probability of the existence of such relationships, and such description being, in fact, substantiated positively by the Protecting Agent and the Declaring Agent appearing before this Court under their declared status and positions vis-a-vis the Suit, both Dr Zahir and Mr Hafizullah now submit that it could not, thereafter, be open to the plaintiff to deny that status to these two agents by reason of the objections now raised. The issue here, both these learned Advocates submit, is a plain and simple one of estoppel. On his part, Mr Ali has argued undeterred that despite the above-referred documents brought on record by the concerned defendants further to the plaintiffs objections, the defendants still appear not to have been readily forthcoming with all relevant information in an alleged attempt at short-circuiting this Court's process of enquiry. While the learned Advocates for the defendants submit that given the recognised and established regulatory power and authority of other relevant and concerned institutions and authorities to determine, certify and annul the legal capacity to act as agents, it would be sufficient for this Court to be satisfied about the prima facie identity, authority and capacity of both these agents to so act for the purposes of this Suit, Mr Ali appears to suggest that it would be for this Court to go a notch farther to enquire in detail into the actual sufficiency of the capacities to act as agents. By that reason, this Court is being asked to undertake an exhaustive and comprehensive exercise of determining and deciding upon the Protecting and Declaring Agents' capacities not only to represent their respective Principals before this Court but also to act per se in their capacities as agents as understood within the various regulatory regimes identified by the plaintiff.
